method: Seven single-attempt independent audio-to-text calls against frozen source clips, compared by controller with complete public captions.
findings: McLatchie presents a maximal-data or Paley-style cumulative case: mundane confirmations support proximity, information and truthfulness; sufficiently detailed unembellished eyewitness claims resist honest mistake; costly proclamation supports sincerity. He explicitly allows combinations of explanatory categories. Paulogia’s core challenge concerns whether the Gospel narratives reach eyewitness testimony at all and whether historical kernels warrant the miraculous portions. Distinguish these steps and do not omit the conditional premise.

Both agree that the minimal-facts material in 1 Corinthians 15 alone leaves the nature of the experiences underdetermined. McLatchie does not defend minimal facts as sufficient; his reliance on Gospel detail is deliberate. Paulogia allows hypothetical historical kernels, including Philip’s origin, without conceding the Gospel authors were eyewitnesses, personally knew eyewitnesses, or wrote uniformly reliable accounts. Conditional grants are not adopted beliefs.

McLatchie offers undesigned coincidences, unexplained allusions and consistent characterization as different but cumulative considerations. Paulogia proposes shared oral tradition, literary dependence, genuine historical kernels, elaboration and coincidence rather than a single rigid written source. The Star Wars analogy is an illustration of story interconnection without truth, not an asserted historical cause of Christian texts. Treat all historical and textual claims as arguments made here, not externally verified facts.

The discrepancy exchange has two explicitly distinguished effects in McLatchie’s account: a genuine error detracts from reliability while increasing independence. Do not attribute the claim that discrepancies only confirm reliability. He allows partial dependence with partial independence and distinguishes well-informed testimony from an infallible document. Paulogia questions discrimination between those accounts and ordinary story development. Do not import the audience-Q&A harmonization of Mary Magdalene into their direct exchange.

The automatic captions and auxiliary recognition remain uncertain in several isolated clauses. Around E1419–E1441 (49 minutes), do not infer an inconsistency or concession from the ambiguous do/don’t wording about a mega-gospel or common oral tradition. At E1660–E1662 the corrupted polarity about honest mistake is unusable; the subsequent complete E1667–E1682 conditional states that such mistake is unlikely. At E2059–E2068, the auxiliary check recovers McLatchie’s ability to give specific examples, Peter and John; do not score the caption “we can’t give specific examples” as a concession. Source claims elsewhere remain assessable; no deduction may rest on these recognition defects.

McLatchie’s persecution argument is explicitly more modest than all twelve died rather than recanting. He names Peter, Paul, the two Jameses and later John; he concedes that Nero’s political scapegoating weakens an inference from the specific executions and that opportunities to recant are not established. The claim is voluntary risks, hardship and general persecution support sincerity, not prove it. Stephen is offered as contextual evidence, not necessarily a resurrection witness. Paulogia accepts a general persecution context and that John requires an account, while asking for the witnesses’ specific claims and independent support.

Paulogia’s “Acts aside” question is hypothetical; McLatchie refuses that exclusion because he defends Acts and also mentions Clement. Do not describe the latter as conceding there is literally no other cited source. Preserve the distinction between reliability as authentic testimony and the truth of its subject matter. McLatchie expressly agrees that confirming mundane facts does not logically entail resurrection, and explains why he still finds those facts evidentially relevant.

Paulogia’s skepticism about miracle testimony is qualified in the late direct exchange: he does not claim philosophical naturalism, and allows that medical documentation could increase a modern miracle claim’s significance. His strongest testimony-only language is later expressed as uncertainty about his own threshold; he also doubts Gospel independence and whether an event’s attribution follows from many reports. McLatchie argues from the purpose of divine signs, religious context and increasing testimonial quantity/quality. The caption “can be a significant objection” at E2660 is missing a negation: the auxiliary check confirms “can’t.” Do not score the corrupted positive claim.

The Barbara Snyder multiple-sclerosis report, Shroud of Turin, John Douglas/McGrew criteria, alien technology, dying/rising religions, audience probability formula and final divine-salvation answer occur in excluded audience Q&A. Do not credit or criticize either side using those answers or the subsequent reaction video. McLatchie’s pre-Q&A references to contemporary miracles and other apologetic categories are retained only at the level presented there; do not import detailed cases from Q&A or outside sources.

Both final summaries repeat the main positions and must be reviewed; score a closing as a distinct move only for genuinely load-bearing argumentative work, not repetition. McLatchie’s closing repeats comparative probability rather than certainty; Paulogia reiterates non-necessity, the single sincere mistaken person hypothesis, his objection to global reliability transfer, and a naturalistic preference. Do not penalize McLatchie for lacking a subsequent chance to answer the last closing.

Public automatic captions were supplemented by seven targeted automated audio-to-text checks. Neither direct human listening nor automatic speaker diarization was performed. Canonical caption words and timestamps remain unchanged. Names and technical terms often contain recognition errors; do not quote or penalize them. Do not silently repair exact quotations. Any remaining selected material uncertainty must be below high confidence and receive required audio verification before adjudication.
